title: Replication
summary: Keeping copies of a database on several machines: leaders and followers, synchronous and asynchronous copying, lag, and quorums.

blocks.p: A database on one machine is lost when that machine's disk fails, and unavailable while it restarts. It can also only serve as many reads as one machine can.

**Replication** keeps a copy of the same data on several machines, called **replicas**. If one fails, another has the data. Reads can be spread across all of them. The hard part is keeping the copies in step while writes keep arriving.

The most common design sends every write to one replica, the **leader**. The leader applies the write and sends a log of its changes to the other replicas, the **followers**, which apply them in the same order. Reads can go to any replica.

With **synchronous** replication, the leader waits until a follower confirms it has the write before telling the client the write succeeded. Having the write is not the same as showing it to reads: in PostgreSQL, `synchronous_commit = on` waits until the follower has saved the change, and `remote_apply` waits until queries on the follower can see it. With **asynchronous** replication, the leader answers at once and sends the change afterwards.
Asynchronous is faster and keeps working when a follower is slow or down. But for a moment after each write, the followers are behind. That delay is **replication lag**.

blocks.caption: A user changes their name, then reloads their profile. With asynchronous replication, the read reaches a follower that hasn't caught up. Reading from the leader avoids it, and so does synchronous replication that waits until the follower has applied the change.

blocks.p: The fix in the third scenario is called **read-your-writes**: after a user writes, send that user's reads to a follower that has caught up to that write, or to the leader. Sending them to the leader "for a few seconds" only works if lag never exceeds those seconds.
If the leader fails, a follower is promoted to leader. This is **failover**. With asynchronous replication, writes the old leader confirmed but hadn't yet sent are lost.

blocks.caption: The leader confirms a write, then fails before sending it on. The promoted follower never received it.

blocks.p: Some databases have no leader. The client sends each write to all N replicas and waits for W of them to confirm. Each read asks R replicas and takes the newest value. When W + R is greater than N, every read asks at least one replica that confirmed the latest completed write. That overlap is all it promises. Two concurrent writes can still conflict, a failed write can leave some replicas with the new value, and the read must still pick the right version. Amazon's [Dynamo paper](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf) goes further. When replicas are down, it writes to stand-ins outside the usual N, a **sloppy quorum**, so overlap is not guaranteed. It keeps conflicting versions for the application to reconcile.

list: **PostgreSQL replicates asynchronously by default.** Its [synchronous replication settings](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/warm-standby.html#SYNCHRONOUS-REPLICATION) make the leader wait for chosen standbys to confirm each commit.

**MySQL does too.** MySQL's [replication documentation](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/replication.html) describes replication as asynchronous by default, with semisynchronous replication as an option.
**A common compromise.** Replicate synchronously to one nearby follower and asynchronously to the rest. One extra copy is always current, and slow followers don't hold up writes.
**Monitor lag.** Lag is usually milliseconds, but it grows under heavy writes or when a follower falls behind. Alert on it, because stale reads look like bugs.

blocks.p: Choose the number of replicas, how many must confirm a write, and how many a read asks.

blocks.caption: A leaderless quorum. Make W + R larger than N and the read overlap becomes at least one replica.

list: Replication keeps copies on several machines for durability, availability and read capacity.
Leader-follower replication sends writes to one leader, which streams changes to followers.
Asynchronous replication is fast but lags, and can lose recent writes on failover.
In a leaderless quorum, W + R > N makes every read ask at least one replica with the latest completed write. It doesn't settle conflicts between concurrent writes.
